result: C. elegans make accept-reject patch choice decisions, initially rejecting several bacterial patches and prioritizing exploration before switching to exploitation. Animals were significantly more likely to stay on patches for longer durations at later time points, with probability of residing on patch increasing significantly after ~10 min.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the work 'convincingly support[s] the idea that the nematode C. elegans uses an accept-reject behavioral strategy' and provides 'strong evidence that worms exhibit...qualitatively distinct behavioral responses.' Reviewer 3 notes the work 'provides strong evidence that C. elegans can make accept-reject decisions upon encountering a food resource.' The editor describes the work as 'convincingly support[ing]' this central claim.

result: The decision to explore or exploit is guided by available sensory information, internal satiety signals, and learned environmental statistics related to bacterial density of recently encountered and exploited patches. Inclusion of satiety-related and history-dependent covariates in the GLM significantly improves prediction of exploitation behavior.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the modeling approach and its conclusions. Reviewer 1 notes 'powerful quantitative modeling approaches including GLMs are used' and that 'accept-reject decisions depend on the quality of the food resource encountered as well as on internally represented features that provide measurements of multiple dimensions of internal state, including feeding status and time.' Reviewer 2 highlights 'the implementation of a generalized linear model (GLM) whose parameters can provide quantitative biological interpretations' as a key novelty.

result: Three distinct patch encounter types were identified based on behavioral clustering: search (encounters lacking slowdown, not detected or ignored), sample (detected encounters with rejection), and exploit (accepted encounters). These are characterized by distinct velocity profiles with search maintaining high velocities (~200 μm/s on and off patch), sample showing intermediate velocities (~114 μm/s), and exploit showing slow velocities (~57 μm/s).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly affirms this classification, stating the work provides 'strong evidence that worms exhibit one of three qualitatively distinct behavioral responses upon encountering a patch: (1) search...below the detection threshold; (2) sample...detect a patch encounter and reduce their motor speed, but do not stay to exploit...and are therefore considered to have rejected it; and (3) exploit...accept the patch and exploit the resource.' The quantitative rigor of this classification is praised by multiple reviewers.

result: Time spent on bacterial patches and probability of residing on patch increased monotonically with bacterial density following a sigmoidal trend. At highest densities (50 and 200), animals spent nearly 100% of time on patches; at lowest densities (0-0.3), animals spent chance levels of time on patch. At intermediate densities (0.5-10), animals initially resided on patches at chance rates before transitioning to more time on patch, with this switch occurring earlier at higher densities. Animals exploited after an average of 4.8-18.7 exploratory encounters at medium densities.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the density-dependent behavioral findings. Reviewer 1 notes 'the probability of these outcomes varies with the density of the patch as well as the prior experience of the animal.' The experimental design and quantitative analysis supporting these density-dependent effects are described as having 'an exceptional level of quantitative rigor and attention to detail' by Reviewer 1.

result: Even in single patch environments, animals initially explore (search and sample) before exploiting in a density-dependent manner, with timing of the switch occurring significantly earlier with increasing bacterial density. This suggests the explore-then-exploit strategy is not specific to patchily distributed environments.
evaluation: While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, this finding is part of the overall behavioral framework that reviewers affirm. The experimental design is described as 'thoroughly vetted' by Reviewer 3, and the work is praised for its 'considerable volume of data to prove their points,' which would include the single-patch experiments supporting the generality of the explore-exploit strategy.

result: Animals with reduced function of non-ciliated mechanoreceptor neurons (mec-4 mutants) behave similarly to wild-type, while animals with reduced function of ciliated chemoreceptor and mechanoreceptor neurons (osm-6 mutants) displayed immediate exploitation even on low-density patches. This suggests ciliated sensory neurons play an important role in evaluating patch density, and when sensation is impaired, animals modify their default strategy to prioritize exploitation.
evaluation: The genetic dissection is implicitly supported as part of the overall framework. Reviewer 1 notes the work uses 'detailed behavioral analysis and rigorous quantitative modeling' and Reviewer 2 highlights the work's ability to 'provide quantitative biological interpretations.' The mutant analysis is part of the mechanistic investigation that reviewers find convincing, though not explicitly discussed in detail.

result: Animals displayed significant deceleration of instantaneous velocity upon encounter with the patch edge, achieving an average deceleration of -19.5 μm/s². This slowdown was statistically significant for both long- and short-duration encounters. Animals maintained significantly lower average velocities on patch (~52 μm/s) compared to off patch (~198 μm/s).
evaluation: These velocity measurements are part of the quantitative behavioral characterization that reviewers praise. Reviewer 1 notes the work is 'carried out with an exceptional level of quantitative rigor and attention to detail' and Reviewer 3 describes the experiments as 'simple and elegant.' The velocity data form the basis for the behavioral state classification that reviewers explicitly support.

result: Animals encountered on average ~8.4 total patches and ~5.3 unique patches during the 1-hr recording. Patch encounters ranged in duration from seconds to tens of minutes and could be classified as either short or long (2+ min) using a Gaussian mixture model.
evaluation: These are descriptive statistics supporting the overall behavioral framework. Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'provide a considerable volume of data to prove their points' and the experimental design is 'thoroughly vetted.' These quantitative measurements are part of the rigorous characterization praised by reviewers.

result: At bacterial densities less than ~0.5, animals do not appear to detect bacterial patches as indicated by on-patch velocities matching those of animals foraging on bacteria-free patches. At bacterial density ~200, bacterial density is comparable to the environments animals experienced during development and immediately prior to the assay.
evaluation: These are methodological and contextual details supporting the density-dependent findings that reviewers affirm. The overall density-dependent framework is explicitly supported by reviewers, and these specific density thresholds are part of that validated framework.

result: In low-density conditions (0-0.3), animals spent nearly all of their time searching on or off patch. With increasing bacterial patch density, animals spent less time searching and more time sampling and exploiting. Animals foraging on high-density patches (50 and 200) almost exclusively exploited.
evaluation: These findings are part of the density-dependent behavioral classification that reviewers explicitly affirm. Reviewer 1 notes the work provides 'strong evidence' for the three behavioral states and their density dependence. These specific observations support the overall framework that reviewers find convincing.

result: An augmentation in exploitation was observed when animals move from low to high density as predicted by the model with history dependence, but not the model without. The lower the density of recently encountered or exploited patches and the higher the density of the current patch, the more likely an animal would be to exploit.
evaluation: These model predictions are part of the GLM framework that reviewers affirm. Reviewer 2 highlights 'the implementation of a generalized linear model (GLM) whose parameters can provide quantitative biological interpretations' as a key contribution. The validation of history-dependent predictions supports the model's utility that reviewers recognize.

result: Reduced efficacy in the evaluation of current patch density in osm-6 mutants also affects learning and memory of patch density. osm-6 mutants display an augmented ability to detect bacterial patches but a diminished ability to assess the bacterial density of those patches.
evaluation: These are interpretations of the osm-6 mutant phenotype that are part of the overall genetic dissection framework. While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, they are consistent with the mechanistic insights that reviewers find valuable in the overall work.

result: C. elegans use sampling as a way of re-evaluating the overall quality of patches available in the environment when a change is detected. The duration of sampling is correlated with the degree of mismatch between current and recently experienced patches. When there is no difference between current and prior experience, animals rarely sample. Animals likely use information learned during sampling to guide subsequent explore-exploit decisions.
evaluation: These interpretations of sampling behavior are part of the overall decision-making framework that reviewers affirm. Reviewer 1 notes the work provides 'an interesting new framework for understanding the ability of the C. elegans nervous system to use sensory information and internal state to implement behavioral state decisions,' which encompasses these sampling-related claims.

result: Bacterial growth during the experiment was negligible.
evaluation: This is a methodological control that reviewers implicitly accept as part of the 'thoroughly vetted' experimental design (Reviewer 3). No concerns are raised about bacterial growth confounding the results.

result: A large portion of short-duration, exploratory encounters were not accompanied by slowdown, especially for the lowest bacterial densities tested.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises concerns about the classification framework, noting 'it is questionable whether worms genuinely do not sense these patches' and that the model 'imposes a prior categorization in trying to distinguish between sensed vs. not-sensed patches.' This suggests uncertainty about whether the lack of slowdown truly indicates non-detection versus a different behavioral response.

result: The results do not imply that C. elegans discretize their experiences into the parameters used in the model. The exact mechanisms underlying the decision to exploit and the best model design require further investigation. It is possible that the density of recently exploited patches is predictive because post-ingestive feedback is required for memory and/or because more distant experiences are remembered.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 expresses concerns about the GLM framing, stating 'it seems odd to reduce past experience to the categories of recently exploited patch, recently encountered patch, and time since last exploitation. This implies the animals have some way of discriminating these past patch experiences and committing them to memory.' The reviewer suggests 'it seems more likely the worm simply has some memory of chemosensation and relative satiety' and that 'the strength of this research could be strengthened by a reassessment of their model that would both simplify it and provide testable timescales of satiety/starvation memory.'
